title: Runtime deep dive — tool outputs, KV sharing & latency vs cost tradeoffs
summary: SE-led runtime deep dive focusing on structured outputs (JSON mode) and function/tool calling overheads. Discussed KV cache sharing across sessions, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem/VPC deployments. Customer has strict latency SLOs (~150ms p50 for short completion slices) and data residency concerns; interested in benchmarking Redwood Dedicated vs private deployment. Agreed on next steps: share microbenchmark sheet, run small end-to-end latency test with their prompt set on Dedicated, and schedule an on-prem pilot scoping call.
topics: KV cache sharing and prefix caching
quantization impact on quality vs throughput
next_steps: Redwood to share microbenchmarks spreadsheet and canary config (Alex)
Customer to provision sample prompts + golden outputs and test dataset (Liam)
Schedule 60-min on-prem scoping with infra (Marissa & Sofia) week of 2026-04-06
action_items: Alex Chen: send microbenchmark spreadsheet and cost/latency worksheet by 2026-03-27
Liam O'Connor: upload 200 prompts + expected JSON shapes by 2026-03-30
Marissa Patel: prepare Dedicated vs Private config checklist and run baseline toy benchmark by 2026-04-02
Sofia Morales: provide network diagram and egress constraints before scoping call (due 2026-04-03)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-25 09:37 PT | Duration 48m | Record: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Marissa Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CTO, VelaMed), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Morales (Infra), Evan Brooks (Product)

[00:00] Alex Chen: All right hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh we know schedules tight so we'll jump in. Quick intros — we're Alex and Marissa from Redwood. 
[00:14] Priya Kapoor: Hi Priya here, thanks. We're trying to understand overheads when we ask the model to return strict json and call external tools, that's been a big pain.
[00:26] Marissa Patel: Great, yeah this is typically where latency can surprise teams — especially when you combine constrained decoding in JSON-mode plus function/tool invocation. We'll walk through what we measure in the runtime and then look at mitigation levers.
[00:39] Liam O'Connor: Quick context — our p50 target for short structured completions is about 150ms, p95 under 400ms. We're currently experimenting on-proxy with a managed endpoint but seeing 280–600ms on typical 100-token JSON payloads.
[00:58] Diego Ramos: Noted. Is that the full round-trip including downstream tool calls or just model-only?
[01:05] Liam O'Connor: Model-only, we strip tool latency out when we measure.
[01:09] Marissa Patel: Okay that clarifies. Two things usually add overhead: constrained decoding enforcement (e.g., JSON-mode) and extra tokens from function schemas plus the function call handshake. Those add both compute and tokenization overhead.
[01:28] [crosstalk] Priya Kapoor: Sorry what do you mean by handshake?
[01:31] Marissa Patel: I mean the runtime may do an extra pass to validate structure, sometimes perform a rerank, or insert stop tokens — small but not zero.
[01:40] Alex Chen: Also worth calling out KV cache effects — if you have prefix caching across similar sessions you can recover a lot of the tokenization and compute, but if every call is new or you rotate keys frequently, cache hit rates plummet.
[01:55] Sofia Morales: Our worst case is stateless calls, because we have to route through a VPC NAT and egress is limited, like 30 concurrent sockets to the managed service, so we may not be able to keep warm persistent connections.
[02:10] Marissa Patel: That's a common constraint in regulated infra. Two options: Dedicated to keep capacity and pinned sessions, or Private on-prem where you run the runtime inside their VPC and avoid external egress. Both have trade-offs.
[02:24] Evan Brooks: Can you quantify the difference for JSON-mode? Roughly how much overhead does constrained decoding add in ms?
[02:31] Marissa Patel: Ballpark: on a 70B-class model on A100-ish hardware, a pure generation baseline might be 60–90ms for a short 100-token completion. Constrained JSON-mode + validation can add 20–60ms depending on how strict the post-processor is and if we run safety/rerank passes. If you add function calling orchestration and schema packing, maybe another 10–30ms. So yes, it adds up beyond your 150ms SLO in some setups.
[03:00] Liam O'Connor: Hmm that matches our numbers. We're currently using int8 quantized variants in staging to lower cost — any gotchas there for JSON?
[03:07] Marissa Patel: Quantization reduces compute latency/throughput but can increase decoding variability — you might see slightly different token probabilities which can alter JSON well-formedness in edge cases. We recommend a small eval suite for critical JSON shapes. Redwood Optimize can flag regressions per prompt.
[03:24] [00:03:25] Priya Kapoor: Is there an option to do partial streaming of the JSON so we return early? Some of our endpoints just need the first few top-level fields.
[03:33] Alex Chen: Yes, streaming is supported. You can stream partial JSON but you need a schema-aware consumer on your side; streaming plus constrained decoding can be tricky but works if you design for chunked parseability.
[03:45] Marissa Patel: Also, batching interacts — if you batch many short queries together to improve throughput, the per-request latency can increase because of queueing. Redwood supports dynamic batching with SLO-aware cutoffs; you can set a max latency budget for a batch.
[03:59] Sofia Morales: We probably need predictable single-request latency more than raw throughput — patient latency bumps are harder for product.
[04:07] Marissa Patel: For that use-case Dedicated or Private with smaller batch windows and lower admission thresholds helps. You lose some throughput efficiency but get tighter p50/p95.
[04:18] [00:04:20] Diego Ramos: Let's walk through a microbenchmark we shared earlier — the spreadsheet — and call out what to measure. We'll want model-only token generation time, JSON-validation time, function-call orchestration time, and end-to-end round-trip including network in their VPC.
[04:36] Liam O'Connor: On network: our network path adds ~20–40ms to outbound calls currently. We'll capture that.
[04:41] Alex Chen: Great. One thing we do in the runtime is prefix KV caching at the block level — for apps that reuse prompt scaffolding we can keep the KV for the first n tokens in memory and only compute the last tokens. That can knock down encoding+decode cost for repeated patterns by 40–70% depending on reuse.
[04:58] Priya Kapoor: How do you garbage collect those caches across users? We have multi-tenant privacy rules.
[05:04] Marissa Patel: Caches can be keyed per-customer and encrypted at rest. They respect retention policies and can be invalidated on deployment/version change or by explicit API. For Private we can expose KMS integration and audit logs.
[05:17] Sofia Morales: Ok good. On cryptography and SOC2 — we need to see audit logs and KMS flow.
[05:22] Alex Chen: We'll attach the security pack. That's part of the next steps.
[05:27] [00:05:30] Evan Brooks: Back to function calls — the tool schema adds tokens to the prompt; do you have strategies to minimize that size?
[05:36] Marissa Patel: Yes, we recommend a schema-slimming approach: only include necessary fields, use compact names, and prefer unary calls when possible. Another strategy is to host the canonical schema server-side and reference an ID in the user prompt — runtime resolves it to the full schema to avoid sending large JSON schemas per request.
[05:56] Liam O'Connor: That could help — we have very verbose tool schemas.
[05:59] Marissa Patel: Also, in Dedicated you can pre-load tool schemas in memory reducing serialization cost.
[06:06] [00:06:10] Diego Ramos: We should talk about reranking and safety filters — those can run in-line or as async post-processors. In-line is simpler but adds to tail latency. Async reduces p95 for the main response but means you need a fallback if the filter flags something.
[06:23] Priya Kapoor: We are sensitive to hallucinations in structured outputs; what's Redwood's approach?
[06:29] Marissa Patel: We use a hybrid approach: syntactic JSON validation first, then semantic checks via small secondary policies, and optionally a low-cost verification model that checks key/value pairs for plausibility before committing. All of those are configurable per-route.
[06:42] Sofia Morales: Does that verification step add significant latency?
[06:45] Marissa Patel: Typically 10–40ms depending on model size; but you can push it async if your product tolerates eventual verification.
[06:54] [00:07:00] Alex Chen: Let's go through a short live example — Marissa will run a constrained decode JSON-mode prompt and we'll watch timings. Marissa, can you kick off test case #12 from the sheet?
[07:09] Marissa Patel: Sure starting now... (keyboard clack)
[07:22] [00:07:22] Marissa Patel: Result: model-only gen time 82ms, JSON validation 28ms, function orchestration 14ms, total model stack 124ms, network round-trip 36ms on our endpoint, so end-to-end 160ms. That's with the baseline quantized model in Dedicated.
[07:42] Liam O'Connor: Ok so that's very close to our target — good to see the breakdown. Which piece is most sensitive if we add stricter schema checks?
[07:50] Marissa Patel: The JSON validation and semantic checks scale with complexity of checks; each extra verification pass is additive. Also rerankers can be expensive if they're large models.
[07:59] [00:08:00] Priya Kapoor: You mentioned KV-sharing earlier — if we enable prefix cache and pin sessions, what kind of p95 improvement might we expect?
[08:09] Marissa Patel: On repeated scaffolds, p95 can drop by up to 40% because we avoid recomputing early layers. Real world depends on reuse. If your prompts vary widely the effect is smaller.
[08:22] Sofia Morales: Are pinned sessions compatible with our VPC NAT constraints?
[08:26] Alex Chen: With Private on-prem, yes — the runtime is inside your network so pinned sessions are trivial. With Dedicated, we offer connection pinning via long-lived tunnels if your firewall allows it.
[08:38] [00:08:40] Diego Ramos: Quantization question — you said earlier variability in output — do you have a recommended evaluation threshold?
[08:45] Marissa Patel: We typically run an A/B of int8 vs fp16 on a representative prompt corpus and accept up to 1–2% structural regression on critical fields, otherwise we avoid aggressive quantization for those routes. Redwood Optimize can automate this check.
[09:00] Liam O'Connor: And memory-wise, quantization helps for throughput but might reduce peak p99 if CPU/GPU kernels saturate?
[09:07] Marissa Patel: Right — quantization reduces bandwidth and memory which tends to increase throughput, but kernel-scheduling and GPU occupancy subtleties can cause some p99 effects; that's why per-hardware profiling is important.
[09:18] [00:09:20] Priya Kapoor: On the idea of streaming partial JSON — do you ever see partial outputs that are syntactically invalid but acceptable because later tokens will fix it? That seems risky.
[09:30] Marissa Patel: Yes it's possible; chunked-parsing strategies help — make each chunk self-contained at field boundaries. Also you can stream coarse-grained sections (e.g., headers first) and then stream details, so you never expose a malformed complete structure.
[09:45] Evan Brooks: Any quick wins if we need to hit the 150ms p50 now?
[09:50] Diego Ramos: Two quick levers: reduce schema size and do prefix caching; second, use Dedicated with a small batch window to avoid queueing. Also consider a smaller model for short structured outputs if quality allows.
[10:06] [00:10:10] Liam O'Connor: We have some latency spikes during load — does Redwood support pre-warming and autoscale policies?
[10:15] Alex Chen: Yes Dedicated supports autoscale with burst capacity and warm pools. For strict SLOs you can reserve a minimum pool size.
[10:23] Priya Kapoor: For Private on-prem, how hands-on is the setup? We have an air-gapped site in EMEA that may need deployment.
[10:31] Marissa Patel: Private is a packaged runtime with installer and an operator; we do a joint install with your infra team. Air-gapped installs require packaging credentials and an offline artifact flow; we have a runbook for that.
[10:44] Sofia Morales: Good.
[10:46] [00:10:48] Diego Ramos: Quick note on observability — we can emit per-token and per-request traces to your tracing backend and Redwood Console will surface per-route cost/latency breakdowns so you can see validation vs generation time.
[10:59] Liam O'Connor: That will help diagnostics a lot.
[11:02] [00:11:05] Marissa Patel: I want to call out one experimental feature: structured-output hints. Instead of strict JSON enforcement we can provide hints to the sampler that bias towards particular field tokens. It's lighter weight than full validation and often reduces the need for heavy post-processing.
[11:20] Priya Kapoor: Is that deterministic?
[11:22] Marissa Patel: Not fully deterministic like a hard constraint, but it's low-latency and reduces repair rates in many corpora. We can test it on your prompts.
[11:33] Evan Brooks: Any notes on cost — does running verification add materially to cost per request?
[11:37] Alex Chen: It does add token compute and model cycles; we quantify that in the microbenchmark sheet. For some customers it's worth it for reduced manual QA.
[11:44] [00:11:45] Liam O'Connor: Ok let's lock in what we'll run: one baseline on Dedicated int8, one on Dedicated fp16, and one on Private on-prem with the same request set; measure model-only, validation, orchestration, and end-to-end.
[11:58] Marissa Patel: Sounds good. We'll also test with prefix cache enabled and disabled to show delta.
[12:05] Sofia Morales: We'll provide network diagram and egress constraints.
[12:10] Alex Chen: Good. A few more quick Qs from me: do you have any hard constraints on key rotation or KMS that would prevent caching?
[12:20] Priya Kapoor: Keys rotate nightly but we can support cache rekeying if you give an API hook.
[12:27] Marissa Patel: That's doable; we'll note that for the runbook.
[12:31] [00:12:35] Diego Ramos: Quick tangent — for function calls that trigger external ops, consider an async approach: return a transaction id quickly and emit the heavy result later. That keeps user-facing latency low.
[12:45] Evan Brooks: We already do async for some long-running ops; good reminder.
[12:49] [00:12:52] Alex Chen: All right we're approaching the last 10 minutes. Any blocker to the proposed next steps?
[12:58] Priya Kapoor: No blockers. We want to see the spreadsheet and test harness.
[13:03] Alex Chen: We'll send that today. Marissa, anything to add before close?
[13:08] Marissa Patel: I'll include config snippets for JSON-mode tuning, an example of a slimmed schema, and notes on streaming-safe chunking. Also a recommended eval harness for quantization A/B.
[13:20] Liam O'Connor: Great.
[13:22] [00:13:25] Diego Ramos: Action items recap: Alex sends spreadsheet; Marissa prepares playbook; customer supplies prompts and infra details.
[13:34] Priya Kapoor: Perfect, thanks all.
[13:35] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the CRM with links and schedule the scoping slot. Bye.

End transcript. Notes: transcription picked up some proper nouns wrong (e.g., may appear as Red wood in raw auto-transcript). There's occasional filler and minor mis-attribution.
